questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Gradient Vector Field of a Function
questions.problem: Find the gradient vector field of the function $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(xz+2y).$
questions.worked_solution:
The gradient vector field of a function $f$ is given by $∇f.$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(xz+2y)) \\  & =z\operatorname{cos}⁡(xz+2y) \\ {f}_{y}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(xz+2y)) \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡(xz+2y) \\ {f}_{z}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(xz+2y)) \\  & =x\operatorname{cos}⁡(xz+2y)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the gradient vector field of $f(x,y,z)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\,j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\,k \\  & =z\operatorname{cos}⁡(xz+2y)\,i+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(xz+2y)\,j+x\operatorname{cos}⁡(xz+2y)\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Gradient Vector Field of a Function
questions.problem: Find the gradient vector field of the function $f(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+4y).$
questions.worked_solution:
The gradient vector field of a function $f$ is given by $∇f.$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+4y)) \\  & =\frac{1}{x+2y} \\ {f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+4y)) \\  & =\frac{2}{x+2y}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the gradient vector field of $f(x,y)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{1}{x+2y}\,i+\frac{2}{x+2y}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find the gradient vector field of the function $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{arctan}⁡(xyz).$
questions.worked_solution:
The gradient vector field of a function $f$ is given by $∇f.$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{arctan}⁡(xyz)) \\  & =\frac{yz}{{x}^{2}{y}^{2}{z}^{2}+1} \\ {f}_{y}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{arctan}⁡(xyz)) \\  & =\frac{xz}{{x}^{2}{y}^{2}{z}^{2}+1} \\ {f}_{z}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{arctan}⁡(xyz)) \\  & =\frac{xy}{{x}^{2}{y}^{2}{z}^{2}+1}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the gradient vector field of $f(x,y,z)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\,j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\,k \\  & =\frac{yz}{{x}^{2}{y}^{2}{z}^{2}+1}\,i+\frac{zz}{{x}^{2}{y}^{2}{z}^{2}+1}\,j+\frac{xy}{{x}^{2}{y}^{2}{z}^{2}+1}\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find the gradient vector field of the function $f(x,y,z)=z{x}^{2}+x{y}^{3}-y{z}^{4}.$
questions.worked_solution:
The gradient vector field of a function $f$ is given by $∇f.$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(z{x}^{2}+x{y}^{3}-y{z}^{4}) \\  & =2xz+{y}^{3} \\ {f}_{y}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(z{x}^{2}+x{y}^{3}-y{z}^{4}) \\  & =3x{y}^{2}-{z}^{4} \\ {f}_{z}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(z{x}^{2}+x{y}^{3}-y{z}^{4}) \\  & ={x}^{2}-4y{z}^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the gradient vector field of $f(x,y,z)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\,j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\,k \\  & =(2xz+{y}^{3})\,i+(3x{y}^{2}-{z}^{4})\,j+({x}^{2}-4y{z}^{3})\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Which of the following diagrams represents the gradient vector field of the function $f(x,y)=\frac{{2}^{x}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)}+{y}^{2}?$
questions.worked_solution:
The gradient vector field of a function $f$ is given by $∇f.$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{{2}^{x}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)}+{y}^{2}) \\  & ={2}^{x} \\ {f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{{2}^{x}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)}+{y}^{2}) \\  & =2y\end{aligned}
$$

 

So, the gradient vector field of $f(x,y)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & ={2}^{x}\,i+2y\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have to sketch the vector field at the points $(-2,1),$ $(0,1),$ and $(2,-1).$

To sketch the vector field at the given points, we substitute their coordinates into the expression for $∇f.$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(-2,1) & ={2}^{-2}\,i+2\cdot (1)\,j=\frac{1}{4}\,i+2\,j \\ ∇f(0,1) & ={2}^{0}\,i+2\cdot 1\,j=i+2\,j \\ ∇f(2,-1) & ={2}^{2}\,i+2\cdot (-1)\,j=4\,i-2\,j\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we draw the vectors starting at the corresponding points and obtain the following diagram:

questions.worked_solution:
The gradient vector field of a function $f$ is given by $∇f.$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}-y) \\  & =2x \\ {f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}-y) \\  & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

So, the gradient vector field of $f(x,y)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =2x\,i-j.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have to sketch the vector field at the points $(-2,1),$ $(0,2),$ and $(2,-1).$

To sketch the vector field at the given points, we substitute their coordinates into the expression for $∇f.$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(-2,1) & =2\cdot (-2)\,i-j=-4\,i-j \\ ∇f(0,2) & =2\cdot (0)\,i-j=-\,j \\ ∇f(2,-1) & =2\cdot 2\,i-j=4\,i-j\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we draw the vectors starting at the corresponding points and obtain the following diagram:

questions.problem: Which of the following diagrams represents the gradient vector field of the function $f(x,y)=2\operatorname{arctan}⁡(xy)?$
questions.worked_solution:
The gradient vector field of a function $f$ is given by $∇f.$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2\operatorname{arctan}⁡(xy)) \\  & =\frac{2y}{{x}^{2}{y}^{2}+1} \\ {f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2\operatorname{arctan}⁡(xy)) \\  & =\frac{2x}{{x}^{2}{y}^{2}+1}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the gradient vector field of $f(x,y)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{2y}{{x}^{2}{y}^{2}+1}\,i+\frac{2x}{{x}^{2}{y}^{2}+1}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Next, we have to sketch the vector field at the points $(-1,1),$ $(0,-2),$ and $(2,0).$

To sketch the vector field at the given points, we substitute their coordinates into the expression for $∇f.$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(-1,1) & =\frac{2\cdot 1}{(-1)^{2}(1)^{2}+1}\,i+\frac{2\cdot (-1)}{(-1)^{2}(1)^{2}+1}\,j=i-j \\ ∇f(0,-2) & =\frac{2\cdot (-2)}{(0)^{2}(-2)^{2}+1}\,i+\frac{2\cdot 0}{(0)^{2}(-2)^{2}+1}\,j=-4\,i \\ ∇f(2,0) & =\frac{2\cdot 0}{(2)^{2}(0)^{2}+1}\,i+\frac{2\cdot 2}{(2)^{2}(0)^{2}+1}\,j=4\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we draw the vectors starting at the corresponding points and obtain the following diagram:

questions.knowledge_point: Using the Relationship Between the Vector Field of a Function and Its Contour Plot
questions.problem: Which of the following could be the gradient vector field of the function $f(x,y)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}?$
questions.worked_solution:
We start by plotting some level curves of the function:

- Setting $f(x,y)=0,$ we get ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=0,$ which gives the origin $O$

- Setting $f(x,y)=1,$ we get ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1,$ a circle of radius $1$ centered at $O$

- Setting $f(x,y)=4,$ we get ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=4,$ a circle of radius $2$ centered at $O$

- $⋯$

Continuing in this way, we get the following contour plot:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14109119/assets/14c453b9fcf4670a2356b730253dd7f411b989abde303f059ebb5a9d559a4eff.png)

Note that $f(x,y)$ increases as we move away from the origin.

Now, we recall the following facts:

- The gradient field vectors of a function $f(x,y)$ always lie perpendicular to its level curves.

- Moreover, the vectors point in the direction where $f(x,y)$ increases.

With this in mind, we can add the vector field to the contour plot, giving the following picture.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14109119/assets/4b20823340d89e0ff4aa2fd65078d3819e8b218419a54ea632c1109e698858ab.png)

So, the corresponding gradient field is as follows:

canonical_examples.problem: Find the gradient vector field of the function $f(x,y) = e^{2x-3y}.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The gradient vector field of a function $f$ is given by $\nabla f.$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({e}^{2x-3y}) \\  & =2{e}^{2x-3y} \\ {f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{2x-3y}) \\  & =-3{e}^{2x-3y}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the gradient vector field of $f(x,y)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =2{e}^{2x-3y}\,i-3{e}^{2x-3y}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The gradient vector field of a function $f$ is given by $\nabla f.$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2{y}^{2}-{x}^{2}) \\  & =-2x \\ {f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2{y}^{2}-{x}^{2}) \\  & =4y\end{aligned}
$$

So, the gradient vector field of $f(x,y)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =-2x\,i+4y\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have to sketch the vector field at the points $(2,1),$ $(-2,1),$ and $(1,-1).$

To sketch the vector field at the given points, we substitute their coordinates into the expression for $\nabla f.$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(2,1) & =-2\cdot 2\,i+4\cdot 1\,j=-4\,i+4\,j \\ ∇f(-2,1) & =-2\cdot (-2)\,i+4\cdot 1\,j=4\,i+4\,j \\ ∇f(1,-1) & =-2\cdot 1\,i+4\cdot (-1)\,j=-2\,i-4\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we draw the vectors at their corresponding points and obtain the following diagram:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14109119/assets/b88c62b154cecaace206248b62f72b8aa1f71662c0427adfbbabd5c2b4738a6b.png)

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14109119/assets/c4d5f211c3bf3d306c6dc14205311c60eeaaf55de89f8af571ec0fa9e5add8a6.png)

 

Which of the above diagrams could be the gradient vector field of the function $f(x,y) = xy?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We start by plotting some level curves of the function:

- Setting $f(x,y) = -1,$ we get $xy = -1,$ which gives the hyperbola $y=-\dfrac 1x$

- Setting $f(x,y) = 0,$ we get $xy = 0,$ that is, the lines $y=0$ and $x=0$

- Setting $f(x,y) = 1,$ we get $xy =1,$ that is, the hyperbola $y=\dfrac 1x$

- Setting $f(x,y) = -2,$ we get $xy =-2,$ that is, the hyperbola $y=-\dfrac 2x$

- $\cdots$

Continuing in this way, we get the following contour plot:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14109119/assets/f95c7ab30b7b02d67ceec039792e649a900dbece2896cc1e63341fcba9fc794f.png)

Note that $f(x,y)$ increases as we move from left to right in the upper half-plane $y > 0,$ and increases as we move from right-to-left in the lower half-plane $y < 0.$

Now, we recall the following facts:

- The gradient field vectors of a function $f(x,y)$ always lie perpendicular to its level curves.

- Moreover, the vectors point in the direction where $f(x,y)$ increases.

With this in mind, we can add the vector field to the contour plot, giving the following picture.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14109119/assets/3d6be27e083bb2e8b508cca31671e5cb4ea4e39b366a99f1dd194a5ea8ffcd3b.png)

So, the corresponding gradient field is as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14109119/assets/996b5678396b4e9a91a4c55697442895331a7a6e4f8ec3eed550ea86845e44f4.png)

       

Therefore, the correct answer is III.
